title: Your Liver Can Regrow 2/3 of Itself in Weeks
description:
Your liver is your biggest internal organ and does more than 500 jobs: it filters your blood, turns toxic ammonia into urea, makes bile to digest fat, stores glycogen, vitamins and iron, and builds clotting proteins. We paint how the liver works, why poop is brown, and how a liver can grow back after up to two thirds is removed, which is what makes living liver donors possible.

Sources:
https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/liver-anatomy-and-functions
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/21481-liver
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/22930-hepatectomy-liver-resection

Animated in the Watercolor Brush style.
pinned_comment: Your liver can lose two thirds of itself and grow back in weeks. Which of its jobs surprised you most: the filter, the bile factory, the pantry, or the regrowing?
topic: Your Liver Explained in Simple Words: the organ that does hundreds of jobs
script:
You could lose two thirds of your liver, and it would actually grow back.
In a few weeks, it's almost back to full size.
No other organ inside you can pull that off.
And while it's doing that, it's still running more than five hundred jobs.
So what is this thing, and how does it do it all?
Let's paint it out, one job at a time.
Chapter one. The biggest organ inside you.
Tuck your hand under your right ribs.
That's roughly where your liver sits.
It's a soft, reddish-brown wedge about the size of a football,
and it weighs around one and a half kilos.
That makes it your biggest internal organ.
And it's always full of blood, about a pint at any moment.
Most of that blood comes straight from your gut,
through one big pipe called the portal vein.
So everything you eat and drink passes through your liver first,
before it reaches the rest of your body.
Chapter two. The filter.
Think of your liver as a security checkpoint.
Inside, it's built from millions of tiny cells called hepatocytes,
lined up in rows like the pages of a book.
Blood seeps slowly between those rows,
and the cells grab anything that shouldn't be there.
Old medicines, leftover chemicals, and alcohol all get broken down here.
Your muscles also make a waste called ammonia,
which is toxic if it builds up.
Your liver turns it into urea,
a much safer waste that your kidneys flush out.
Chapter three. The bile factory.
Your liver also makes bile, a greenish-yellow juice,
up to about a litre of it every day.
Bile works a lot like dish soap.
It breaks big blobs of fat into tiny droplets,
so your gut can actually digest them.
Between meals, the bile waits in a little pouch called the gallbladder.
And here's a weird one.
Bile carries leftovers from old red blood cells,
and that's what turns your poop brown.
Chapter four. The pantry.
After a meal, your liver packs extra sugar away
as a starch called glycogen.
Then, between meals or while you sleep,
it turns that glycogen back into sugar,
so your brain never runs out of fuel.
It also keeps a stash of vitamin A, vitamin D,
vitamin B twelve, and iron, for later.
And it builds proteins your blood needs,
including the ones that make a cut stop bleeding.
Chapter five. The comeback organ.
Now back to that superpower.
Doctors can remove up to two thirds of a healthy liver,
and the rest starts growing right away.
The cells that are left simply divide,
and the liver can get back most of its size in a few weeks.
That's why living donors are possible.
A healthy adult gives part of their liver to someone who needs it,
and both pieces grow into full-size livers.
And scientists are still working out exactly how it knows when to stop.
So the next time you eat a meal,
remember the quiet organ under your ribs,
filtering, storing, building, and regrowing,
more than five hundred jobs, all at once.
Next time, what really happens if you swallow chewing gum?
Does it actually stay inside you for seven years?
key_facts: The liver is the largest internal (solid) organ, about 1.5 kg / 3 lb (Cleveland Clinic)
It performs more than 500 functions (Johns Hopkins Medicine)
It holds about a pint (~13%) of the body's blood at any moment; most of its blood arrives via the portal vein from the gut (Johns Hopkins)
Liver makes bile (roughly up to a litre a day), stored in the gallbladder; bilirubin from old red blood cells gives stool its brown colour
It converts ammonia to urea, stores glycogen, vitamins A, D, B12 and iron, and makes clotting proteins (Johns Hopkins)
Up to two thirds of a healthy liver can be removed; it can regenerate in as little as a few weeks, sometimes several months; in living donation both parts grow back to full size (Cleveland Clinic)
